newsitem.title: PERU: Gunfire breaks peace at Peru siege site.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire breaks peace at Peru siege site.

text.p: Three bursts of gunfire shattered the calm on Monday around the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima where heavily armed Marxist rebels were holding 74 hostages for the 27th day.

Witnesses and policemen said they believed the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels used assault rifles to fire into the air from within the residence after spotting what appeared to be a police helicopter hovering overhead.
"The helicopter came too close, so they opened fire," one policeman at the site told Reuters.

The shots sent birds scattering in panic across the front of the residence and journalists ducking for cover. Some police crouched in alert positions, weapons at the ready, but most police remained calm and Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig entered the residence minutes later as peace returned.

Red Cross spokesman Cecilia Baux later confirmed there were no injuries after the mid-morning gunfire. "We wish to underline once more the need to strictly maintain the calm in the surroundings of the residence," she added.
The rebels had fired gunshots into the air on several previous occasions during the crisis in an apparent effort to attract attention and make their presence felt.

Tentative contacts between the government and the rebels continued Monday after hopes were dashed Sunday for a second face-to-face meeting between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa. But both sides remained intransigent in their bargaining positions.

The MRTA announced early Monday it had a reply to the government's proposal to set up a "guarantor committee" to oversee talks to end the crisis. Using its now familiar mode of communication, the rebels placed a sign in an upper window of the residence asking Palermo to allow a local television network to enter the building to enable the MRTA to "make a public reply to the proposal."
There was no immediate response from the government.

Palermo made the proposal Sunday after Cerpa told him in a written note to cancel a planned meeting unless he was prepared to discuss liberating jailed MRTA members. The curt message, delivered by Red Cross officials, ended brief hopes of a swift end to the crisis and showed how little the sides had shifted their positions since the siege began Dec. 17.

President Alberto Fujimori has repeatedly ruled out the demand to release MRTA prisoners, dismissing it as "terrorist blackmail." But he has floated the possibility of transporting the rebels to another country if they lay down their arms and release all the remaining captives.

"My government's immovable position from the start is that we will not release prisoners. Why would we free terrorists? We're negotiating safe passage, and there are various ways to do that," Fujimori told the weekly U.S. newsmagazine Time in an interview published Monday.
Fujimori added that "no one can tell how long this (crisis) could go on" and said he could not rule out the use of force on either side.

He said the presence of his brother, Pedro Fujimori, among the hostages was not affecting his judgment. "(It is) neither harder nor easier. If he weren't a hostage, my stand would be the same. In these circumstances, one should act with a cool head and repress natural emotions. He's my brother, but I have to act as the president."

Fujimori also reiterated that the crisis was an isolated incident. "The crisis could affect tourism, but I think investors know perfectly well what the country's social and economic situation is. They know this doesn't mean a resurgence of terrorism. Terrorism is disappearing in Peru; there are only a few pockets left in the jungle."
